identity.description: Histogram-based gradient-boosted tree ensemble with leaf-wise (best-first) growth. Bins features into discrete histograms and grows the highest-gain leaf next, making it the fastest strong tabular learner at scale — with native missing-value and native categorical handling.

emits.note: classification; well-ranked but often miscalibrated — see calibration placement
native per-row via predict(pred_contrib=True) (SHAP-style feature contributions); global importances also native

max_depth.note: -1 = unconstrained; capping it is the standard small-n guard against leaf-wise overfit

invariances.why: splits are threshold comparisons on histogram bins; rescaling a feature relabels bin boundaries but yields the identical partition of rows
histogram bins are built from the feature's value ORDER (quantile-style binning), so any monotone transform produces the same bin membership and hence the same trees
use_missing is on by default — at each split NaNs are routed to whichever side maximizes gain, so no imputation is required
categorical splits use Fisher's optimal-grouping — categories sorted by gradient statistics then split as if ordered — provided columns are declared via category dtype or categorical_feature
a non-parametric ensemble makes no assumption about the marginal or error distribution
histogram binning + GOSS/EFB were designed for large n and dominate there; leaf-wise growth at default num_leaves=31 overfits sharply on small datasets
tree predictions are piecewise-constant; outside the training range the prediction is clamped to the nearest leaf

featureStats.why: leaf-wise growth fits the highest-gain leaf regardless of depth, so low n/p lets single leaves memorize noise — a gate signal toward simpler families or hard num_leaves/max_depth caps
severe imbalance makes accuracy meaningless, shifts the honest metric to PR-AUC/lift, and suggests is_unbalance/scale_pos_weight
high missingness is where the learned per-split NaN routing is an advantage worth citing over impute-then-linear
Fisher-grouped categorical splits can overfit very-high-cardinality columns (docs recommend min_data_per_group/cat_smooth) — cardinality decides native-categorical vs alternative encodings

modelMetrics.why: if a linear model ties the GBT, the added variance/opacity of boosting is not earning its keep — a commit-linear signal
one feature owning most importance is the leakage-dominance signature the promotion gate blocks
leaf-wise growth's variance surfaces directly as train-vs-valid divergence — the knob-level signal that num_leaves/min_child_samples need tightening

edgeCases.behavior: leaf-wise growth at default num_leaves memorizes rows; unstable CV

edgeCases.condition: string/object dtype column not declared as category
edgeCases.behavior: fit raises ValueError (only numeric or category dtypes accepted)
per-category gradient groups become tiny and overfit
library warning; leaf budget can never be reached

driver.wrapperNeeds: none (sklearn-compatible fit/predict/predict_proba); categorical columns must arrive as pandas category dtype or be named via categorical_feature

placementClaims.why: per-split learned NaN routing makes upstream imputation unnecessary and sometimes harmful (destroys the missingness signal)
monotone-transform-invariant: log/rank/box-cox cannot change bin membership or split structure
scale-insensitive by mechanism; standardization is wasted compute
one-hot defeats the native Fisher-grouped categorical splits and fragments high-cardinality columns into weak sparse binary splits (docs explicitly recommend raw categories over one-hot)
